propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review under section 72 of IRPA of a delegate's decision denying permanent residence on humanitarian grounds.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review, pursuant to section 72 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA], of a decision made by a delegate of the Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship (the “Delegate”) to deny the Applicant’s application for permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate grounds (“H&C application”) pursuant to subsection 25(1) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review application under IRPA section 72 of a delegate's denial of permanent residence on humanitarian grounds.

propositions.text: Applicant Demilade Kayode Oladele is Nigerian, married to Canadian Jennifer Oladele, with four children including a stepson.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, Demilade Kayode Oladele, was born in Nigeria and is a citizen of that country. He is married to a Canadian citizen, Jennifer Oladele. They have four children: Jayden (the Applicant’s stepson), Manessah, Ethan and Grace.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant is Nigerian, married to a Canadian, with four children including a stepson.

propositions.text: Applicant entered Canada in 2005 with a fraudulent passport and made a refugee claim.
propositions.quote: In October 2005, the Applicant entered Canada with a fraudulent passport and made a refugee claim.

propositions.text: In 2008, section 44 reports were made against Applicant under IRPA paragraphs 35(1)(a) and 37(1)(a).
propositions.quote: In 2008, section 44 reports were written against the Applicant pursuant to paragraphs 35(1)(a) and 37(1)(a) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: In August 2010, Immigration Division issued deportation order for inadmissibility under those provisions.
propositions.quote: In August 2010, the Immigration Division (“ID”) issued a deportation order based on inadmissibility under those two provisions.

propositions.text: Applicant unsuccessfully sought judicial review of referral and inadmissibility determination.
propositions.quote: The Applicant unsuccessfully sought judicial review of the referral to an inadmissibility hearing and the subsequent determination.

propositions.text: Applicant's Pre-Removal Risk Assessment application in October 2010 was denied in December 2010.
propositions.quote: In October 2010, the Applicant made a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (“PRRA”) application but this application was denied in December of that year.

paragraphs.summary: The court states applicant entered Canada fraudulently, faced inadmissibility reports and deportation, unsuccessfully sought judicial review, and had a denied PRRA application.

propositions.text: Inadmissibility based on Applicant's involvement with Neo Black Movement of Africa (NBMA).
propositions.quote: The basis of inadmissibility is the Applicant’s involvement with the Neo Black Movement of Africa (“NBMA”).

propositions.text: Immigration Division found reasonable grounds NBMA committed crimes against humanity and Applicant was a member complicit in those crimes.
propositions.quote: The ID found reasonable grounds to believe that the NBMA committed crimes against humanity, and that the Applicant had membership in this organization and was complicit in those crimes.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found Applicant inadmissible due to NBMA membership and complicity in crimes against humanity.

propositions.text: Applicant married a Canadian woman after arrival but they separated; her sponsorship application was denied due to Applicant's common law relationship with current wife.
propositions.quote: The Applicant married a Canadian woman after his arrival in Canada, but they eventually separated. That woman applied to sponsor him for permanent residence, but that application was denied when the Applicant formed a common law relationship with his current wife.

paragraphs.summary: The court states applicant's first Canadian marriage ended, and her sponsorship was denied due to his new common law relationship.

propositions.text: Applicant met current wife in 2008, became involved in 2009, had son Manessah in April 2011, and married in July 2011.
propositions.quote: The Applicant and his current wife met in 2008, and became romantically involved in 2009. In April 2011, Mrs. Oladele gave birth to their son Manessah. In July 2011, the couple married.

paragraphs.summary: The court states applicant met current wife in 2008, had son in 2011, and married her that year.

propositions.text: In October 2010, current wife applied to sponsor Applicant; Applicant submitted H&C application in January 2011 requesting inadmissibility waiver.
propositions.quote: In October 2010, Mrs. Oladele applied to sponsor the Applicant for permanent residence. In January 2011, the Applicant submitted an H&C application, in which he requested a waiver of inadmissibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court states current wife applied to sponsor applicant in 2010; applicant submitted H&C application in 2011.

propositions.text: Applicant was deported to Nigeria in December 2011; wife and children visited but returned to Canada without him due to difficult conditions.
propositions.quote: In December 2011, the Applicant was deported to Nigeria. His pregnant wife, Jayden and Manessah visited him shortly thereafter. Conditions in Nigeria made the trip difficult and the Applicant’s wife and children returned to Canada without him.

paragraphs.summary: The court states applicant was deported in 2011; wife and children visited but returned to Canada without him due to conditions.

propositions.text: In June 2012, Mrs. Oladele gave birth to Ethan.
propositions.quote: In June 2012, Mrs. Oladele gave birth to Ethan.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mrs. Oladele gave birth to Ethan in June 2012.

propositions.text: In August 2012, IRCC denied sponsorship application because Applicant was residing outside Canada.
propositions.quote: In August 2012, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (“IRCC”) denied the sponsorship application because the Applicant was residing outside of Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRCC denied sponsorship in 2012 because applicant lived outside Canada.

propositions.text: In September 2014, wife and children joined Applicant in Uganda on temporary student visa, causing financial and emotional hardship.
propositions.quote: In September 2014, the Applicant’s wife and children joined him in Uganda, where he was living under a temporary student visa. This caused the family financial and emotional hardship. Mrs. Oladele had resigned from her job in Canada, sold their house and liquidated assets.

paragraphs.summary: The court states wife and children joined applicant in Uganda in 2014, causing financial and emotional hardship.

propositions.text: Trip to Uganda was difficult; family had employment trouble; wife had medical issues including vision problems and back pain; she returned to Canada for testing but went back to Uganda against advice.
propositions.quote: The trip to Uganda was difficult. The Applicant and his wife had trouble finding employment. Jayden suffered a medical issue. Mrs. Oladele began to experience trouble with her vision. She returned to Canada for medical testing, where doctors determined that the vision impairment might be caused by her diagnosis of multiple sclerosis. Against her doctor’s wishes, Mrs. Oladele returned to Uganda. Mrs. Oladele also suffers from lower back pain associated with a degenerative disc disease.

paragraphs.summary: The court states family faced hardships in Uganda including medical issues for wife and son, and wife returned to Uganda against medical advice.

propositions.text: In December 2015, Applicant requested urgent decision on H&C application.
propositions.quote: In December 2015, the Applicant requested an urgent decision on the H&C application.

paragraphs.summary: The court states applicant requested urgent decision on H&C application in December 2015.

propositions.text: In April 2016, Mrs. Oladele was pregnant with Grace.
propositions.quote: In April 2016, Mrs. Oladele was pregnant with Grace.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mrs. Oladele was pregnant with Grace in April 2016.

propositions.text: By 2016, family exhausted finances; Applicant's student visa expired; he returned to Nigeria alone; family returned to Canada and lived in one-bedroom apartment with wife's mother; wife job searched despite pregnancy and medical issues; stepson had anxiety and paranoia.
propositions.quote: By 2016, the family had exhausted their finances. The Applicant’s student visa expired and he returned to Nigeria. His family did not accompany him due to the poor and dangerous conditions in that country. The family returned to Canada without him. They moved into a one-bedroom apartment with Mrs. Oladele’s mother. Mrs. Oladele began a job search despite her pregnancy and medical condition. Jayden experienced symptoms of anxiety and paranoia.

paragraphs.summary: The court states family exhausted finances by 2016; applicant returned to Nigeria; family returned to Canada and faced hardships.

propositions.text: In May 2016, Applicant applied for writ of mandamus but settled with Minister.
propositions.quote: In May 2016, the Applicant applied to this court for a writ of mandamus but settled with the Minister of IRCC (the “Minister”).

paragraphs.summary: The court states applicant applied for writ of mandamus in May 2016 but settled with Minister.

propositions.text: In December 2016, the H&C application was denied.
propositions.quote: In December 2016, the H&C application was denied.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the H&C application was denied in December 2016.

propositions.text: In January 2017, Mrs. Oladele gave birth to Grace.
propositions.quote: In January 2017, Mrs. Oladele gave birth to Grace.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mrs. Oladele gave birth to Grace in January 2017.

propositions.text: In May 2010, IRCC Officer referred H&C application to Delegate due to possible grounds to grant but lacked authority to waive inadmissibility.
propositions.quote: In May 2010, an IRCC Officer (the “Officer”) referred the H&C application to the Delegate because she found there may be sufficient grounds to grant the application, but did not have delegated authority to waive inadmissibility.

propositions.text: Officer removed two country-conditions files from Applicant's submissions because positive decision factors were based on establishment, BIOC and reunification in Canada.
propositions.quote: Prior to forwarding the application to the Delegate, the Officer removed two files of country-conditions documents from the Applicant’s submissions because “…the factors supporting the positive decision were based on establishment, BIOC and reunification in Canada.”

propositions.text: Officer found more evidence supporting positive decision than negative.
propositions.quote: The Officer found that there “was far more evidence supporting a positive decision than a negative one”.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker's officer referred H&C application to Delegate, removed country-conditions files, and found more evidence supporting positive decision.

propositions.text: Delegate's reasons quote section 44 reports and ID's inadmissibility decision extensively.
propositions.quote: The Delegate’s reasons for decision contain extensive quotes from the section 44 reports and the ID’s inadmissibility decision.

propositions.text: Delegate notes severity of Applicant's admitted NBMA activities including rioting and hijacking government vehicles.
propositions.quote: The Delegate notes the severity and seriousness of the activities the Applicant admitted to partaking as a member of the NBMA, including rioting and hijacking government vehicles.

propositions.text: Delegate notes NBMA's role in aiding Applicant's travel to Canada.
propositions.quote: She also notes the NBMA’s role in aiding the Applicant’s travel to Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker's delegate quoted reports and found Applicant's NBMA activities severe and that NBMA aided his travel to Canada.

propositions.text: Delegate’s reasons contain extensive quotes from Mrs. Oladele and her mother’s recent letters about family hardships and medical issues.
propositions.quote: the Delegate’s reasons contain extensive quotes from Mrs. Oladele and her mother’s recent letters. These submissions speak to the family’s hardships in Uganda, Jayden’s medical issue, her pregnancy, unemployment, her medical challenges and the harm the family has suffered.

paragraphs.summary: The Delegate’s reasons include extensive quotes from Mrs. Oladele and her mother about family hardships and medical issues, as found by the earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: Delegate questions Applicant’s decision to marry and have children under deportation order but finds no evidence he is a bad parent or harms children’s best interests.
propositions.quote: The Delegate questions the Applicant’s decision to marry and have children while under a deportation order, but finds no evidence that the Applicant is a bad parent, or that the children’s best interests are not served by his presence in their lives.

propositions.text: Delegate acknowledges growing up without a father is not ideal but common, and recognizes family’s financial hardship mitigated by social assistance and babysitting.
propositions.quote: She acknowledges that growing up without a father is not ideal, but that is a situation children regularly face in this day and age. She also recognizes the family’s financial hardship, but finds this is mitigated by the availability of social assistance, the ability for Mrs. Oladele to seek employment and the capacity of Jayden to babysit his siblings.

paragraphs.summary: The Delegate questions the Applicant’s family decisions but finds no evidence of bad parenting and recognizes financial hardship is mitigated, as found by the earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: Delegate makes little mention of documentary evidence about Nigeria conditions or children’s capacity to adapt there.
propositions.quote: The Delegate makes little mention of the documentary evidence regarding conditions in Nigeria, or about the children’s capacity to adapt to life there.

paragraphs.summary: The Delegate makes little mention of documentary evidence about Nigeria or children’s adaptation capacity, as found by the earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: Delegate found Applicant established financially and socially in Canada, no criminal record, no evidence of future criminal activity if returned.
propositions.quote: The Delegate found that the Applicant had established himself financially and in the community during his time in Canada, that he had no criminal record in Canada and there was no evidence he would partake in any criminal activity should he return to Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The Delegate found the Applicant financially and socially established in Canada with no criminal record or evidence of future criminality, as found by the earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: Delegate concluded H&C factors not in Applicant’s favour despite best interests of wife and children to not be separated.
propositions.quote: The Delegate concluded that the balance of H&C factors was not in the Applicant’s favour. She noted that it was in the best interests of the wife and children to not be separated from him;

propositions.text: Delegate questioned Applicant’s decision to marry and have children under deportation order.
propositions.quote: however, she questioned his decision to marry and have children while under a deportation order.

propositions.text: Delegate listed factors against granting application: admission to riots and hijacking, NBMA travel facilitation, fraudulent newspaper clipping, false spousal application.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, she listed the factors against granting the application: his admission to leading riots and hijacking public transportation as a member of the NBMA; his travel to Canada was facilitated by the NBMA; he submitted a fraudulent newspaper clipping to the ID; and he pursued a spousal application under false pretenses.

paragraphs.summary: The Delegate concluded H&C factors were not in Applicant’s favour, questioned family decisions, and listed adverse factors, as found by the earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: Issues: breach of procedural fairness by Officer’s removal of submissions and Delegate’s comments on family decisions; unreasonableness of Delegate’s BIOC analysis, inadmissibility reassessment, and factor weighing.
propositions.quote: The issues are: Was there a breach of procedural fairness due to: the Officer’s removal of submissions prior to forwarding the file to the Delegate? the Delegate’s comments regarding the Applicant’s family decisions? Was the Delegate’s decision unreasonable due to: her failure to particularize the interests of each child and consider country conditions in the BIOC analysis? her failure to reassess inadmissibility in light of Ezokola and B010? her weighing of the factors for and against allowing the H&C application?

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies issues of procedural fairness breaches and unreasonableness in the Delegate’s decision on family comments, BIOC analysis, inadmissibility, and factor weighing.

propositions.text: Standard of review for procedural fairness is correctness, per SCC cases Khosa and Khela.
propositions.quote: The standard of review for procedural fairness is correctness (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at para 43; and Mission Institution v Khela, 2014 SCC 24 at para 79).

paragraphs.summary: The standard of review for procedural fairness is correctness, per Supreme Court of Canada precedents Khosa and Khela.

propositions.text: Standard of reasonableness applies to review of decision under IRPA subsection 25(1), per SCC Kanthasamy.
propositions.quote: A standard of reasonableness applies when reviewing the exercise of decision pursuant to subsection 25(1) of the IRPA (Kanthasamy v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61 [Kanthasamy] at para 44).

paragraphs.summary: A standard of reasonableness applies to review of decisions under IRPA subsection 25(1), per SCC Kanthasamy.

propositions.text: Applicant argues procedural fairness denied because Officer removed country-conditions evidence before referral, so Delegate decided on incomplete record.
propositions.quote: In his written submissions, the Applicant argues that he was denied procedural fairness because the Officer removed country-conditions evidence from the file before referring the matter to the Delegate, contrary to procedural guidelines, and then the Delegate rendered a decision based on the incomplete record.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues procedural fairness was denied because the Officer removed country-conditions evidence before referral, leading to an incomplete record for the Delegate.

propositions.text: Respondent argues Delegate had sufficient country-conditions evidence despite missing two documents, which were not highly relevant.
propositions.quote: In the Respondent’s written submissions, the Respondent argues that despite the missing two documents, the Delegate still had sufficient country-conditions evidence before her when the decision was made and the excluded submissions are not highly relevant to the final outcome.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues the Delegate had sufficient country-conditions evidence despite two missing documents, which were not highly relevant.

propositions.text: Applicant agrees all country-conditions submissions are in Certified Tribunal Record but asks court to find they were not before Delegate due to Officer’s removal comment.
propositions.quote: However, during oral arguments the Applicant agreed that all country-conditions submissions were in the Certified Tribunal Record (“CTR”). The Applicant asked the Court to find on a balance of probabilities that these materials were not before the Delegate when she made her decision, on the grounds that the Officer mentioned removing country-conditions documents before forwarding the matter to the Delegate.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant agrees all country-conditions submissions are in the record but asks court to find they were not before the Delegate due to Officer’s removal comment.

propositions.text: No breach of procedural fairness; country-conditions evidence likely before Delegate when decision made.
propositions.quote: In my opinion, there was no breach of procedural fairness. The country-conditions evidence is in the CTR and was likely before the Delegate when she made her decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes no breach of procedural fairness occurred; country-conditions evidence was likely before the Delegate.

propositions.text: Baker requires full and fair consideration of issues and meaningful opportunity to present evidence in H&C applications.
propositions.quote: In Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 SCR 817 [Baker], the Supreme Court of Canada (“SCC”) held that procedural fairness in H&C applications requires a full and fair consideration of the issues, and a meaningful opportunity to present the various types of evidence relevant to their case and have it fully and fairly considered (Baker, at para 32).

propositions.text: Legitimate expectations may determine procedural fairness requirements (Baker at para 26).
propositions.quote: As well, a person’s legitimate expectations may determine what procedures the duty of fairness requires in given circumstances (Baker, at para 26).

paragraphs.summary: Baker requires full and fair consideration and meaningful opportunity to present evidence in H&C cases; legitimate expectations affect procedural fairness.

propositions.text: H&C Guidelines require officers to forward entire file including submissions to Delegate, who must review all applicant’s submissions.
propositions.quote: Citizenship and Immigration Canada’s Inland Processing Operational Manual, “Humanitarian and compassionate consideration” [H&C Guidelines] provides that if an officer refers a case to a delegated decision-maker, he or she must forward a copy of the entire file including any submissions related to the case, and the delegate must review all of the applicant’s submissions: Referrals to delegated decision-makers - Procedures for officers A case should be referred to a delegated decision maker when both of the following apply: • you do not have the delegated authority to grant a requested exemption and • you believe that the H&C considerations might justify an exemption. When referring a case to a delegated decision maker do the following: […] Review submissions from client to determine if applicant remains inadmissible. If applicant remains inadmissible, ensure all extrinsic evidence and applicant’s submissions are included in the package to the delegated decision maker. […] If the applicant is inadmissible […], prepare a package containing copies of relevant documents for the H&C decision-maker, including all of the following: •a copy of the entire H&C case file including any submissions related to the case Procedures for the delegated decision-maker Receive the H&C application package from the referring officer. Review all material submitted by the applicant […].

paragraphs.summary: H&C Guidelines require officers to forward entire file including submissions to Delegate, who must review all applicant’s submissions.

propositions.text: Officer ignored procedures and did not forward two country-conditions documents to Delegate, an unreasonable decision risking incomplete record.
propositions.quote: The Officer ignored these procedures and did not forward two country-conditions documents to the Delegate. She reasoned that the documents were not related to the factors supporting a positive decision. This was not a reasonable decision to make, given that it could have caused the Delegate to not have the entirety of the Applicant’s submissions before her when she made her decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer ignored procedures by not forwarding two country-conditions documents, risking an incomplete record before the Delegate.

propositions.text: Respondent failed to disclose Officer’s exclusion of evidence; Applicant discovered this only via access to information request.
propositions.quote: That mistake was exacerbated by the Respondent’s failure to disclose the Officer’s decision to exclude evidence. Only through an access to information request did the Applicant discover that evidence had been removed from the file before it was sent to the Delegate.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Respondent failed to disclose the Officer’s exclusion of evidence, discovered only by Applicant’s access to information request.

propositions.text: Administrative procedural rules may create legitimate expectations that they will be followed (Agraira).
propositions.quote: In Agraira, the SCC stated that the existence of administrative rules of procedure may give rise to a legitimate expectation that such procedures will be followed (Agraira v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2013 SCC 36 at para 95).

propositions.text: This Court has applied legitimate expectations doctrine where procedural guidelines were not followed, even if guidelines are not binding precedents.
propositions.quote: As well, this Court has previously applied the doctrine of legitimate expectations where procedural guidelines have not been followed, even though such guidelines are not legal precedents or binding on the Court (Serhii v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 841).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes SCC’s Agraira ruling on legitimate expectations from procedural rules and this Court’s application of that doctrine to non-binding guidelines.

propositions.text: Decision made on incomplete record constitutes denial of natural justice (Pramauntanyath).
propositions.quote: Furthermore, in Pramauntanyath v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FC 174, this Court held that a decision made on the basis of an incomplete record constitutes a denial of natural justice.

paragraphs.summary: A decision made on an incomplete record constitutes denial of natural justice, per Pramauntanyath.

propositions.text: Applicant admits all country-conditions submissions are in CTR; nothing suggests Delegate lacked full submissions except Officer’s removal comment.
propositions.quote: However, as noted above, the Applicant now admits that all of his country-conditions submissions are present in the CTR. Except for the Officer’s comment with respect to removing documents from the file, there is nothing to suggest that the entirety of the Applicant’s country-condition submissions were not before the Delegate when she made her decision. It is the Delegate’s decision that is under review, not the Officer’s.

propositions.text: It is the Delegate’s decision under review, not the Officer’s; no evidence Delegate lacked full submissions.
propositions.quote: It is the Delegate’s decision that is under review, not the Officer’s.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant admits all country-conditions submissions are in the record; the court notes only the Delegate’s decision is under review, not the Officer’s.

propositions.text: Officer’s actions did not cause breach of procedural fairness by Delegate.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the actions of the Officer did not cause a breach of procedural fairness by the Delegate.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Officer’s actions did not cause a breach of procedural fairness by the Delegate.

propositions.text: Delegate's analysis is tainted by speculation and objections about marriage and children under deportation order
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the Delegate’s analysis is tainted by speculation and objections with respect to his decision to marry and have children while subject to a deportation order.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness required Delegate to allow Applicant to respond to objections
propositions.quote: procedural fairness required the Delegate to give the Applicant a chance to respond to those objections.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Delegate's analysis is speculative about family decisions and procedural fairness required a chance to respond.

propositions.text: Delegate made comments on family decisions including relocation to Uganda and parenting disapproval
propositions.quote: the Delegate refers to the family’s decision to relocate to Uganda as a “poor [decision] with respect to the care of their children.”

propositions.text: Delegate 'reads between the lines' of letter suggesting disapproval and entitlement sense
propositions.quote: She “reads between the lines” of a letter written by Mrs. Oladele’s mother, suggesting that the mother disapproved of her daughter and son-in-law’s parenting decisions, and that Mrs. Oladele and her mother have a “peculiar sense of entitlement

propositions.text: Delegate notes Applicant knew he lacked legal status when deciding to have children
propositions.quote: I note that Mr. and Mrs. Oladele would have been aware that Mr. Oladele did not have legal status and may never have been able to reside legally in Canada at the time they decided to have children together.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant refers to Delegate's comments on family relocation, parenting disapproval, and knowledge of illegal status when having children.

propositions.text: Delegate speculates Applicant married and had children hoping family ties would prevent deportation
propositions.quote: Whether these decisions were motivated by a hope that family ties would prevent his deportation is possible

propositions.text: Delegate finds these behaviors hard to reconcile with genuine concern for offspring
propositions.quote: these behaviours are difficult to reconcile with someone who had the interests of his own off-spring at heart.

propositions.text: Delegate concludes granting permanent residence is not justified due to negative factors and family decisions
propositions.quote: when balanced against the negative factors in this case, granting Mr. Oladele’s permanent residence on this basis is not, in my opinion, justified.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant notes Delegate speculates family decisions motivated by deportation avoidance and denies permanent residence as unjustified.

propositions.text: Delegate permitted to consider that H&C grounds result from Applicant's own actions
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the Delegate was permitted to take into consideration the fact that the grounds of the H&C application were the result of the Applicant’s own actions.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues Delegate could consider H&C grounds arose from Applicant's own actions.

propositions.text: Delegate entitled to consider parenting decisions and marriage/births under deportation order
propositions.quote: The Delegate was entitled to consider factors such as parenting decisions and that the marriage and births occurred while the Applicant was under a deportation order.

propositions.text: Legault case states Minister can refuse H&C if circumstances discredit applicant or encourage illegal entry
propositions.quote: The Minister...is definitely authorized to refuse the exception requested by a person who has established the existence of humanitarian and compassionate grounds, if he believes...circumstances surrounding his entry and stay in Canada discredit him or create a precedent susceptible of encouraging illegal entry in Canada.

propositions.text: Minister may consider that H&C grounds result from applicant's own actions
propositions.quote: the Minister is at liberty to take into consideration the fact that the humanitarian and compassionate grounds that a person claims are the result of his own actions.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent cites Legault: Delegate may consider parenting and marriage under deportation and that H&C grounds may result from applicant's actions.

propositions.text: Delegate's comments were part of weighing factors, no animus or pre-decided outcome found
propositions.quote: They do not show an animus towards the Applicant, nor do they show that the Delegate approached the analysis with the outcome already decided.

propositions.text: No apprehension of bias found
propositions.quote: I do not find there was any apprehension of bias.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Delegate's comments were balanced and no bias or pre-decided outcome existed.

propositions.text: Applicant had opportunity to explain relationship circumstances
propositions.quote: the Applicant had the opportunity to make submissions to explain the circumstances of his relationship.

propositions.text: Delegate identified fact of starting family under deportation order, not speculative conclusion
propositions.quote: the Delegate is not reaching a speculative conclusion, but is identifying the fact that the Applicant decided to start a family while under a deportation order.

propositions.text: Delegate entitled to weigh family decisions negatively; no procedural unfairness
propositions.quote: The Delegate was entitled to weigh those factors negatively. There was no procedural unfairness.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Applicant had chance to respond, Delegate's conclusion factual not speculative, no procedural unfairness.

propositions.text: Delegate's BIOC analysis flawed for not considering country conditions and particularizing each child
propositions.quote: First, the Delegate’s best interests of the child (“BIOC”) analysis was flawed because the Delegate failed to consider country conditions and particularize the interests of each child.

propositions.text: Delegate erred by not reassessing inadmissibility after SCC decisions Ezokola and B010
propositions.quote: Second, the Delegate erred by declining to reassess inadmissibility in light of the SCC’s decisions in Ezokola...and B010.

propositions.text: Weighing of H&C factors was unreasonable for other reasons
propositions.quote: Finally, the weighing of the different H&C factors was unreasonable for various other reasons.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Delegate's BIOC analysis flawed, inadmissibility not reassessed post-SCC, and H&C factors weighing unreasonable.

propositions.text: Delegate reasonably assessed children's interests together and considered country conditions
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the Delegate reasonably assessed the children’s interests simultaneously, given their similarities, and that country conditions were sufficiently considered.

propositions.text: ID's prior inadmissibility finding is res judicata; no issue with paragraph 37(1)(a) inadmissibility
propositions.quote: the ID’s prior finding on paragraph 35(1)(a) inadmissibility is res judicata and there is no issue with respect to the ID’s finding on paragraph 37(1)(a) inadmissibility.

propositions.text: Court should not re-weigh H&C factors
propositions.quote: Finally, the Court should not re-weigh the different H&C factors.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues Delegate reasonably assessed children and country conditions, inadmissibility findings final, and no re-weighing needed.

propositions.text: Delegate unreasonably failed to particularize unborn child's interests and consider country conditions for all children
propositions.quote: the Delegate unreasonably failed to particularize the interests of the Applicant’s unborn child and failed to consider country conditions with respect to all the children’s interests.

propositions.text: Delegate's decision unintelligible as impact of Ezokola unclear
propositions.quote: the Delegate’s decision is unintelligible, because the impact of Ezokola on her analysis is unclear.

propositions.text: No need to consider reasonableness of H&C factors balancing due to above
propositions.quote: For those reasons, it is not necessary to consider whether the Delegate’s balancing of the H&C factors was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Delegate failed to particularize unborn child's interests, consider country conditions, and decision unclear on Ezokola impact.

propositions.text: Delegate failed to particularize BIOC for four children by age, capacity, needs, maturity, experiences, relationships
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that the Delegate failed to particularize the best interests of the four children based on age, capacity, needs, maturity, personal experiences and relationships with the Applicant.

propositions.text: Delegate failed to consider BIOC with respect to evidence of Nigeria conditions
propositions.quote: Delegate failed to consider the BIOC with respect to the Applicant’s evidence of conditions in Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Delegate failed to particularize BIOC for children and consider Nigeria country conditions.

propositions.text: If no distinguishing factors, reasonable to consider children's interests together
propositions.quote: if there is no distinguishing factor that makes one child’s interest different from that of another, then it is reasonable to consider their interests together.

propositions.text: Delegate sufficiently considered country conditions
propositions.quote: the Delegate sufficiently considered country conditions in her analysis.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues reasonable to consider children's interests together and country conditions were sufficiently considered.

propositions.text: Delegate reasonably singled out oldest child with specific issues and treated two close-age children similarly
propositions.quote: the Delegate reasonably singled out the oldest child, who has issues specific to him, while giving similar treatment to the two children who are close in age and experience.

propositions.text: Unreasonable for Delegate to omit needs of unborn child and fail to consider country conditions for BIOC
propositions.quote: it was unreasonable for the Delegate to not mention the needs specific to an unborn child. It was also unreasonable for the Delegate to fail to consider country conditions with respect to the BIOC.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Delegate reasonably treated older and close-age children but unreasonably omitted unborn child's needs and country conditions.

propositions.text: BIOC analysis requires attentiveness to children's rights, best interests, and hardship from negative decision
propositions.quote: A BIOC analysis requires “…attentiveness and sensitivity to the importance of the rights of children, to their best interests, and to the hardship that may be caused to them by a negative decision…” (Baker, at para 74).

paragraphs.summary: BIOC analysis requires attentiveness to children's rights, best interests, and hardship from negative decisions (Baker).

propositions.text: BIOC analysis is contextual, responsive to each child's age, capacity, needs, maturity (Kanthasamy)
propositions.quote: Such an analysis is highly contextual because of the multitude of factors that may impinge on the child’s best interest; therefore, it must be done in a manner responsive to each child’s particular age, capacity, needs and maturity (Kanthasamy, at para 25).

propositions.text: Child's development level guides BIOC application in context (Kanthasamy)
propositions.quote: The child’s level of development will guide its precise application in the context of a particular case (Kanthasamy).

paragraphs.summary: BIOC analysis is contextual and guided by child's development, age, capacity, needs, and maturity (Kanthasamy).

propositions.text: H&C Guidelines list factors for BIOC: age, dependency, establishment, links, country conditions, medical issues, education, gender (Kanthasamy)
propositions.quote: The H&C Guidelines set out relevant considerations for this inquiry (Kanthasamy, at para 40): the age of the child; the level of dependency between the child and the H&C applicant; the degree of the child’s establishment in Canada; the child’s links to the country in relation to which the H&C assessment is being considered; the conditions of that country and the potential impact on the child; medical issues or special needs the child may have; the impact to the child’s education; and matters related to the child’s gender.

paragraphs.summary: H&C Guidelines list BIOC factors including age, dependency, establishment, links, country conditions, medical issues, education, gender.

propositions.text: No rigid formula for BIOC; substance over form (Semana)
propositions.quote: there is no specific formula or rigid test to be used by immigration officers in a BIOC analysis; form should not be elevated over substance (Semana v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 1082 at para 25).

paragraphs.summary: BIOC analysis has no rigid formula; substance is prioritized over form (Semana).

propositions.text: Four children affected: Jayden (12), Manessah (5), Ethan (4), Grace (unborn)
propositions.quote: Here, there are four children affected by the H&C decision. Jayden is the Applicant’s stepson and was twelve years old when the decision was made, Manessah was five years old, Ethan was four years old and Grace was not yet born.

paragraphs.summary: Four children affected: Jayden (12), Manessah (5), Ethan (4), Grace (unborn).

propositions.text: Delegate reasonably considered Jayden's psychological, medical issues, ties to Canada, and status difficulties in Nigeria
propositions.quote: The Delegate refers to a psychological assessment of Jayden that showed he suffers from sadness and anxiety due to the absence of the Applicant. As well, she refers to a recent medical situation with Jayden that occurred in Uganda. Furthermore, she notes that Jayden still has ties to his biological father and grandmother within Canada. Finally, she notes that it may be difficult for Jayden to obtain status in Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: Delegate reasonably considered Jayden's psychological, medical issues, Canadian ties, and Nigerian status difficulties.

propositions.text: Delegate made fewer references to Manessah and Ethan, noting their confusion about leaving home and family
propositions.quote: The Delegate made fewer specific references to Manessah and Ethan. The Delegate notes their confusion about having left their home, family and friends behind, but that Jayden seems better able to understand the situation.

paragraphs.summary: Delegate made fewer references to Manessah and Ethan, noting their confusion about leaving home and family.

propositions.text: It was reasonable for the Delegate to single out Jayden and treat Manessah and Ethan similarly due to age and specific issues.
propositions.quote: I find that it was reasonable for the Delegate to single out Jayden and treat Manessah and Ethan similarly.

propositions.text: Jayden is older and has specific issues; Manessah and Ethan are similar in age and experiences living mostly without their father.
propositions.quote: Jayden is much older and has issues that are specific to him. Manessah and Ethan are about the same age and their experiences are similar to each other in that they have lived most of their lives without their father.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it reasonable for the Delegate to treat Jayden differently from Manessah and Ethan due to age and experiences.

propositions.text: Grace has specific interests as an infant needing care, no physical contact with Applicant, and too young for video relationship.
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that Grace has interests that are specific to her: she is an infant that requires a great deal of attention and care; she has had no physical contact with the Applicant; and she is too young to establish a relationship with him via video communication.

propositions.text: The court agrees that Grace has specific interests as an infant requiring care and no physical contact with Applicant.
propositions.quote: I agree.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues Grace has specific infant needs and no contact; the court agrees with this argument.

propositions.text: BIOC analysis applies equally to unborn children (Hamzai v Canada).
propositions.quote: The BIOC analysis applies equally to unborn children (Hamzai v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FC 1108 at para 33).

propositions.text: Failure to consider best interests of unborn child may be unreasonable (Li and Melendez cases).
propositions.quote: A failure to take into consideration the best interests of an unborn child may, in and of itself, be unreasonable (Li v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2016 FC 451 at para 25; and Melendez v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2016 FC 1363 at paras 36-37).

paragraphs.summary: The court cites case law that BIOC applies to unborn children and ignoring their interests may be unreasonable.

propositions.text: The Delegate fails to discuss how decision impacts Grace, mentioning her interests only with other children.
propositions.quote: However, the Delegate fails to discuss how her decision impacts Grace. The Delegate simply mentions Grace’s interests together with those of the other children.

propositions.text: Delegate stated limited evidence that Mr. Oladele is not a good parent and best interests of children might not be served by his presence.
propositions.quote: For example, the Delegate stated, “[t]here is therefore limited evidence before me that Mr. Oladele is not a good parent and that the best interests of Jayden, Manasseh, Ethan and the unborn child might not best be served by having him present in their lives on a day-to-day basis in Canada.”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Delegate did not specifically address Grace's interests, only grouping her with other children.

propositions.text: Delegate's reasons were not responsive to Grace's particular age, capacity, needs, and maturity as required by Kanthasamy.
propositions.quote: The Delegate’s reasons were not responsive to Grace’s “…particular age, capacity, needs and maturity” (Kanthasamy, at para 25).

propositions.text: Grace's interests were not well identified or examined with attention as required by Kanthasamy.
propositions.quote: Nor were Grace’s interests “‘…well identified and defined’ and examined ‘with a great deal of attention’ in light of all the evidence” (Kanthasamy at para 39).

propositions.text: Delegate did not mention infant needs or impact of moving to Nigeria or father living abroad, treating infant needs same as older children.
propositions.quote: The Delegate did not mention of the needs of an infant child, nor how an infant child might be impacted by moving to Nigeria or her father living in a different country. It was unreasonable to consider the needs of an infant child as if they are the same needs as children who are 4-12 years older.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Delegate failed to properly consider Grace's specific infant needs and impacts, contrary to legal standards.

propositions.text: Delegate fails to consider country conditions in BIOC analysis except limited references to cultural adaptation and status issues.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the Delegate fails to consider country conditions in her BIOC analysis. In the section titled “Best interests of the children”, there is no mention of conditions in Nigeria, except for a reference to Mrs. Oladele’s struggle to adapt culturally and Jayden’s difficulty in obtaining status.

propositions.text: In 'Country conditions in Nigeria' section, Delegate does not consider impact on children except quoting Applicant's submissions on poor education.
propositions.quote: In the section titled “Country conditions in Nigeria”, the Delegate does not consider how country conditions might impact the interests of the four children, except for a quote from the Applicant’s own submissions where he stated, “…The United States Department of State reports that education in Nigeria is very poor….Both Mr. and Mrs. Oladele state that it would not be in the children’s best interests to relocate to Nigeria.”

propositions.text: Delegate does not explore country conditions further or mention children in that part or in 'Balancing' section.
propositions.quote: The Delegate does not explore this further nor does she mention any of the four children in this part of her decision. Finally, in the section titled “Balancing”, the Delegate fails to mention country conditions entirely.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Delegate failed to consider country conditions' impact on the children in her BIOC analysis.

propositions.text: Delegate was required to be sensitive to children's interests and evidence but was not sensitive to country conditions or unborn child's interests.
propositions.quote: As noted above, the Delegate was required to be alert, alive and sensitive to the children’s interests and examine those interests in light of all the evidence. The Delegate was not sensitive to the impact of country conditions on the children. Nor was the Delegate sensitive to the particular interests of the Applicant’s unborn child.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Delegate failed to be sensitive to children's interests and country conditions as required.

propositions.text: The Delegate’s BIOC analysis was unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the Delegate’s BIOC analysis was unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Delegate's BIOC analysis was unreasonable.

propositions.text: Applicant argues Delegate failed to consider inadmissibility grounds in light of SCC decisions Ezokola and B010 and no clear inadmissibility determination under IRPA 35(1)(a).
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that the Delegate failed to consider the grounds for inadmissibility in light of the SCC’s recent decisions in Ezokola and B010, and that there is no clear determination of the Applicant’s inadmissibility with respect to paragraph 35(1)(a) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the Delegate failed to consider inadmissibility grounds per recent SCC decisions and lacks clear inadmissibility determination.

propositions.text: Respondent argues ID's inadmissibility findings are res judicata and cannot be challenged due to case law changes; inadmissibility under IRPA 37(1)(a) stands.
propositions.quote: The Respondent argues that the ID’s findings of inadmissibility are res judicata, and applicants cannot challenge the validity of lawful decisions simply because of subsequent changes to the case law. Furthermore, the finding of inadmissibility under paragraph 37(1)(a) of the IRPA stands unimpeached.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues inadmissibility findings are res judicata and remain valid despite case law changes.

propositions.text: Delegate’s reasons are unintelligible regarding Ezokola's impact on inadmissibility and H&C analysis.
propositions.quote: In my opinion, the Delegate’s reasons are unintelligible because the impact of Ezokola on the Applicant’s inadmissibility and the Delegate’s H&C analysis are unclear.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Delegate's reasons unclear on Ezokola's impact on inadmissibility and H&C analysis.

propositions.text: It was reasonable for Delegate not to mention B010 as it concerns different IRPA provision and is dissimilar to Applicant's case.
propositions.quote: Regarding B010, it was reasonable for the Delegate to not mention this decision in her reasons. That case dealt with paragraph 37(1)(b) of the IRPA. In particular, whether individuals could be found to have engaged in human smuggling merely by aiding others without seeking some financial or other material benefit. That case and provision are dissimilar from paragraph 37(1)(a) of the IRPA, which deals with membership in a criminal organization, and do not have a significant bearing on the outcome of the Applicant’s H&C application.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it reasonable the Delegate did not mention B010 as it concerns a different IRPA provision.

propositions.text: Ezokola SCC changed test for complicity to knowing and significant contribution to crime or group's criminal purpose.
propositions.quote: In Ezokola, the SCC changed the test for complicity with regard to crimes against humanity or war crimes. Complicity requires a knowing and significant contribution to the crime or criminal purpose of a group (Ezokola, at para 68).

propositions.text: Before Ezokola, complicity required personal and knowing participation (Ramirez case).
propositions.quote: Prior to Ezokola, complicity required personal and knowing participation (Ramirez v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1992] 2 FCR 306 at paras 4-22).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Ezokola changed complicity test to knowing and significant contribution, replacing prior personal participation test.

propositions.text: Ezokola test applies to IRPA 35(1)(a) but not to membership under IRPA 37(1)(a) (Chung case).
propositions.quote: The new test for complicity applies to paragraph 35(1)(a) of the IRPA (Concepcion v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 544 at paras 9-15). However, it does not apply to “membership in an organization” pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(a) of the IRPA (Chung v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 16 at para 84).

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ezokola test applies to IRPA 35(1)(a) but not to membership under IRPA 37(1)(a).

propositions.text: Court disagrees with Respondent that issue estoppel precludes reassessment of ID's inadmissibility finding under IRPA 35(1)(a).
propositions.quote: I disagree with the Respondent that the doctrine of issue estoppel precludes a reassessment of the ID’s finding of paragraph 35(1)(a) inadmissibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees that issue estoppel bars reassessment of inadmissibility under IRPA 35(1)(a).

propositions.text: FCA in Oberlander held issue estoppel may not apply if it causes injustice; applicant entitled to re-determination post-Ezokola.
propositions.quote: The application of issue estoppel post-Ezokola was considered by the Federal Court of Appeal (“FCA”) in Oberlander v Canada (Attorney General), 2016 FCA 52 [Oberlander]. If the criteria for issue estoppel are met, the Court retains a residual discretion to not apply the doctrine where it could work an injustice (Oberlander at para 16, citing Danyluk v Ainsworth Technologies Inc, 2001 SCC 44 at para 80). In that case, the Court was satisfied that the application of issue estoppel with respect to Ezokola worked an injustice and the applicant was entitled to a re-determination of his citizenship revocation.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Oberlander that issue estoppel may be refused to avoid injustice, allowing re-determination post-Ezokola.

propositions.text: Hamida case found H&C decision needed reconsideration due to Ezokola change in law.
propositions.quote: In Hamida v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 98, this Court considered the application of issue estoppel with respect to an H&C application that was refused prior to Ezokola. The Court found that the decision needed to be reconsidered in light of the change of law set out in Ezokola (Hamida at para 40).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Hamida required reconsideration of H&C decision due to Ezokola law change.

propositions.text: H&C decision-makers have discretion to consider Ezokola's impact on inadmissibility findings and must consider intervening SCC decisions.
propositions.quote: Moreover, it is clear that decision-makers on H&C applications have discretion to consider the impact of Ezokola on previous findings of inadmissibility. Officers making these decisions must be satisfied that applicants meet the requirements of the IRPA and should consider the relevance of an intervening SCC decision (NK v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 1040 at paras 19-21).

propositions.text: H&C decision unreasonable if reasons do not clarify if inadmissibility assessed under Ezokola test (Aazamyar case).
propositions.quote: A H&C decision will be unreasonable if it is impossible to ascertain from the decision-maker’s reasons whether the applicant’s inadmissibility may or may not have been assessed upon the refined test set out in Ezokola (Aazamyar v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 99 at paras 39-41).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains H&C decision-makers must consider Ezokola and clarify inadmissibility assessment to avoid unreasonableness.

propositions.text: Sabadao states res judicata cannot bar H&C applications; officers must consider new jurisprudence to balance H&C grounds.
propositions.quote: In my opinion, the following statement of the Court’s applies here (Sabadao v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 815 at para 22 [Sabadao]): […] res judicata cannot be a bar in the context of an H&C application. […] an officer ought to consider recent jurisprudential developments, not for the purpose of indirectly or implicitly overturning a final decision, but for the purpose of balancing that factor with other H&C grounds. […] If, as a result of a new jurisprudential interpretation of an inadmissibility provision, the Applicant’s refugee claim might have turned out differently, it is obviously a factor that the Officer should have taken into consideration in assessing his H&C claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Sabadao that res judicata does not bar H&C applications and officers must consider new jurisprudence.

propositions.text: Delegate acknowledged Ezokola but found Applicant's complicity unclear and inadmissibility under section 37 of IRPA accepted.
propositions.quote: The admissibility hearing revealed that Mr. Oladele’s evidence was contradictory. He admitted to membership in the NBMA and his participation in riots and hijackings of public transportation (non-violent according to Mr. Oladele) at the port of entry but when it became clear that his status in Canada was at stake he changed his story in order to minimize his participation in NBMA activities. Therefore the degree of his participation in any activities which could render him complicit in crimes against humanity remain nebulous. What is clear is that Mr. Oladele’s testimony on the subject may not be reliable; for example the ID member found that Mr. Oladele had submitted a fraudulent newspaper article in an attempt to exculpate himself. In terms of whether post-Ezokola Mr. Oladele would be found to be inadmissible for complicity in crimes against humanity, in my opinion, this question cannot be answered in the context of this decision. If Mr. Oladele had arrived in Canada in 2013 instead of 2005 it is true that the Immigration Division’s analysis may have been slightly different and a more detailed analysis of where and when crimes against humanity in Nigeria in relation to where and when Mr. Oladele was a member of the NBMA may have been adduced at the hearing (which sat on 4 separate occasions) and may have been included in the ID’s reasons. This is not to say that the information linking Mr. Oladele to crimes against humanity more directly does not exist but it is not obvious from the record before me. Regardless of the complicity in crimes against humanity argument, in terms of the section 37 analysis there has been no significantly new jurisprudence on membership in a criminal organization which would call the member’s finding into question. I therefore accept that Mr. Oladele is inadmissible, at a minimum, pursuant to section 37 of IRPA for his involvement in a cult, namely the NBMA and that he was an active participant in this criminal organization from which he derived significant benefits.

paragraphs.summary: The Delegate acknowledged Ezokola but found Applicant's complicity unclear and accepted inadmissibility under section 37 of IRPA.

propositions.text: The Delegate mentions the NBMA twice as a factor against granting the application.
propositions.quote: in her list of factors against granting the application, the Delegate mentions the NBMA twice

propositions.text: Mr. Oladele admitted leading riots in Nigeria as NBMA member, recognizing their violence and hijacking public transport.
propositions.quote: Mr. Oladele admitted to leading riots in Nigeria when he was a member of the NBMA, recognizing that these riots were often violent and to hijacking public transportation

propositions.text: Mr. Oladele's travel to Canada was facilitated by a human smuggling network linked to the NBMA, which committed serious crimes.
propositions.quote: Mr. Oladele’s travel to Canada was facilitated by using a human smuggling network linked to the NBMA – an organization which committed serious domestic crimes in Nigeria if not crimes against humanity

paragraphs.summary: The Delegate cited NBMA involvement and related crimes as factors against the application, including riots and smuggling, as found by the earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: The Delegate's reasons are unintelligible regarding the role of paragraph 35(1)(a) inadmissibility in balancing H&C factors.
propositions.quote: these reasons are unintelligible. It is unclear to what the extent paragraph 35(1)(a) inadmissibility played a role in the Delegate’s balancing of H&C factors

propositions.text: Clarity on the role of inadmissibility is imperative because participation in crimes against humanity could determine the H&C outcome.
propositions.quote: Clarity on this point is imperative because participation in crimes against humanity is a serious accusation that by itself could determine the outcome of an H&C application

propositions.text: A negative H&C decision would significantly impact the Applicant's family and children.
propositions.quote: a negative H&C decision would have significant impact on the Applicant’s family and children

propositions.text: The Applicant is entitled to know the weight given to Ezokola and inadmissibility and how it was balanced against favourable H&C factors.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is entitled to know the weight given to Ezokola and paragraph 35(1)(a) inadmissibility and how it was balanced against the H&C factors in his favour

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Delegate's reasons unclear on inadmissibility's role and says the Applicant deserves clarity on its weight and impact on H&C factors.

propositions.text: The impact of the change in law should be balanced with other factors, citing Sabadao.
propositions.quote: The impact of the change in law should be balanced with other factors (Sabadao)

propositions.text: The Delegate's final balancing does not mention Ezokola and only finds the Applicant inadmissible under paragraph 37(1)(a).
propositions.quote: there is no mention of Ezokola in the Delegate’s final balancing of factors. The Delegate has merely found that that “at a minimum” the Applicant is inadmissible pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(a)

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Delegate failed to mention Ezokola in final balancing and only found inadmissibility under paragraph 37(1)(a).

propositions.text: The Delegate's balancing refers to Applicant's admission to riots but earlier acknowledged he no longer admits this.
propositions.quote: the Delegate’s balancing of factors refers specifically to the Applicant’s admission to taking part in riots, but earlier in her reasons she acknowledged that the Applicant no longer admits this

propositions.text: The Delegate stated the degree of Applicant's participation in crimes against humanity remains nebulous and unanswered in this decision.
propositions.quote: the degree of his participation in any activities which could render him complicit in crimes against humanity remain nebulous” and “this question cannot be answered in the context of this decision

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Delegate inconsistently referred to Applicant's riot admission and acknowledged uncertainty about his participation in crimes against humanity.

propositions.text: The Delegate was not in the same position as the ID to review inadmissibility comprehensively.
propositions.quote: the Delegate was not in the same position as the ID to conduct a comprehensive review of inadmissibility

propositions.text: The Delegate must clarify how Ezokola impacted her decision, following a nuanced approach from Figueroa.
propositions.quote: the Delegate must provide more clarity on how Ezokola impacted her decision. This Court has suggested the following, more nuanced approach (Figueroa v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 673 at para 31)

propositions.text: The nuanced approach requires considering prior inadmissibility findings and the gravity of inadmissibility in light of submissions.
propositions.quote: This requires the Minister’s Delegate to do two things: (1) consider a prior inadmissibility finding in light of any submissions to determine whether that finding still stands; and (2) consider the gravity of the inadmissibility in light of the submissions

paragraphs.summary: The court says the Delegate must clarify Ezokola's impact, applying a nuanced approach considering prior inadmissibility and its gravity.

propositions.text: Even if the Delegate cannot determine if prior inadmissibility stands, clarity on Ezokola's impact is needed.
propositions.quote: Even if the Delegate cannot determine whether or not the previous inadmissibility finding still stands, the Applicant and this Court need clarity with regard to the impact of Ezokola on the Delegate’s decision

propositions.text: Paragraph 35(1)(a) inadmissibility significantly impacts the H&C application and family hardship if denied.
propositions.quote: Paragraph 35(1)(a) inadmissibility has a significant impact on this H&C application, and there is no question that the family will suffer substantial hardship if the application is denied

paragraphs.summary: The court finds clarity on Ezokola's impact is needed due to significant inadmissibility impact and family hardship risk.

propositions.text: The Delegate's reasons are unintelligible and therefore unreasonable.
propositions.quote: I find that the Delegate’s reasons are unintelligible and therefore unreasonable

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is granted and the matter is referred to a different Delegate for reconsideration.
propositions.quote: The application is granted and the matter is referred to a different Delegate for reconsideration

propositions.text: There is no question for certification.
propositions.quote: There is no question for certification

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Delegate's reasons unintelligible and unreasonable, grants the application, and refers the matter for reconsideration.
